title: Expert Merging in Sparse Mixture of Experts with Nash Bargaining
claim: Expert outputs in different MoE models show distinct, layer-dependent similarity patterns, revealing diverse and non-uniform expert interaction dynamics.
layout: 3x3 grid of heatmaps, one row per model, shared colorbars
description: A 3x3 grid of cosine-similarity heatmaps between experts, drawn with a diverging blue-white-red colormap from -1 to 1. Each row is one model and has its own colorbar on the right. Top row: Swin-MoE, Layers 2, 5 and 8, with 8 experts (e1–e8). Its off-diagonal values are near zero, so the experts are nearly uncorrelated. Middle row: Switch-Transformer, Layers 3, 5 and 7, also 8 experts. Warm off-diagonal blocks of moderate positive correlation appear. Layer 7 also has a distinct blue negative-correlation band for e1 and e2 against the other experts. Bottom row: Qwen-MoE, Layers 5, 7 and 9, with about 60 experts. The grid is finer, with streaks and local clusters near the diagonal in Layers 5 and 7. At Layer 9 it is mostly clean, with a bright red diagonal. The eye goes first to the strong red diagonals and the blue band in the middle-right panel.
caption: Cosine similarity of expert outputs in Swin-MoE [ref] (top), Switch-Transformer [ref] (middle), and Qwen-MoE [ref] (bottom). Swin-MoE shows stable mid-layer features, Switch-Transformer exhibits dynamic routing at Layer 8, and Qwen-MoE yields robust final representations at Layer 9--highlighting diverse expert interaction patterns.
abstract: Existing expert merging strategies for Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE) typically rely on input-dependent or input-independent averaging of expert parameters, but often lack a principled weighting mechanism. In this work, we reinterpret expert merging through the lens of game theory, revealing cooperative and competitive dynamics among experts. Based on this perspective, we introduce Nash Merging of Experts (NAMEx), a novel framework that incorporates Nash Bargaining into the merging process, enabling more balanced and efficient collaboration among experts. Additionally, we incorporate complex momentum into NAMEx to accelerate expert propagation with theoretical guarantees for convergence. Extensive experiments across language modelling, text classification, image classification, and zero-shot robustness under data corruption show that NAMEx consistently outperforms competing methods while integrating seamlessly with popular MoE architectures. Finally, we demonstrate NAMEx's scalability by applying it to large-scale systems, including Qwen1.5-MoE (14B) and DeepSeek-MoE (16B), where it proves effective in both zero-shot and fine-tuning settings. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/anh147/NAMEx.
